decisions.reason: The endpoint, transition, and key update differ: after client Finished both client sending and receiving keys change, while after server Finished only the server sending key changes and application data becomes sendable.
The illegal_parameter outcomes match, but the conditions test different relations: selection outside ClientHello.cipher_suites versus a ServerHello cipher-suite change from HelloRetryRequest.
They map different CipherSuite members to different wire values: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 to 0x1301 and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 to 0x1303.
The conditions select different signature families, and the PSS rule specifically constrains the signed digest while the PKCS1-v1_5 rule defines that scheme family's corresponding hash.
They map different AlertDescription members to different values: certificate_expired to 45 and certificate_required to 116.
Negotiating cryptographic modes and parameters across the handshake is broader than selecting cryptographic parameters specifically during the Key Exchange phase.
They map different ContentType members to different values: change_cipher_spec to 20 and application_data to 23.
The placement checks concern different extensions and allowed message sets: signature_algorithms in CH/CR versus early_data in CH/EE/NST.
The records and allowed values differ: an initial ClientHello record permits legacy_record_version 0x0301 or 0x0303, while a ServerHello record requires 0x0303.
They map different AlertDescription members to different values: unknown_ca to 48 and unknown_psk_identity to 115.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: supported_groups in CH/EE versus oid_filters only in CR.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: use_srtp in CH/EE versus signature_algorithms_cert in CH/CR.
They map different AlertDescription members to different values: certificate_unknown to 46 and certificate_required to 116.

One constrains the declared byte size of a fixed-length vector, while the other rejects an encoded vector whose runtime byte length contains a partial element; the declaration and parsing conditions are not equivalent.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: heartbeat in CH/EE versus signature_algorithms_cert in CH/CR.
The bounds apply to different Certificate fields and widths: CertificateEntry.extensions permits 0..65535 bytes, while certificate_request_context permits 0..255 bytes.
The same retry ClientHello triggers separate recomputations of different fields: obfuscated_ticket_age values versus PSK binder values.
The opaque vectors are different fields with different minima: OIDFilter.certificate_extension_values permits empty content, while KeyShareEntry.key_exchange requires at least one byte.
Although both terminate with unexpected_message, one trigger is a specifically premature KeyUpdate handshake message and the other is receipt of an unexpected record type.
They order different preference lists: supported protocol versions versus named groups.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: client_certificate_type in CH/EE versus oid_filters only in CR.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: supported_versions in CH/SH/HRR versus signature_algorithms_cert in CH/CR.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: status_request in CH/CR/CT versus early_data in CH/EE/NST.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: server_certificate_type in CH/EE versus psk_key_exchange_modes only in CH.
They map different ExtensionType members to different values: client_certificate_type to 19 and server_certificate_type to 20.
The opaque vectors are different fields with different minima: Cookie.cookie requires 1..65535 bytes, while OIDFilter.certificate_extension_values permits 0..65535 bytes.
One orders a client's Certificate before its CertificateVerify; the other requires a certificate-authenticating server to send CertificateVerify at all.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: psk_key_exchange_modes only in CH versus early_data in CH/EE/NST.
The receiver and message differ: a server ignores an unrecognized ClientHello parameter, while a client ignores an unrecognized NewSessionTicket extension.
The limits apply to different fields and have different minima: OfferedPsks.identities starts at 7 encoded bytes, while CertificateEntry.extensions starts at 0.
The vectors carry different element types and have different maxima: ClientHello supported_versions is 2..254 bytes, while supported_signature_algorithms is 2..65534 bytes.
The source states, received messages, and target states differ: WAIT_EE plus EncryptedExtensions enters WAIT_CERT_CR, while WAIT_CERT_CR plus CertificateRequest enters WAIT_CERT.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: supported_versions in CH/SH/HRR versus oid_filters only in CR.
The bounds apply to different Certificate fields and widths: certificate_request_context permits 0..255 bytes, while certificate_list permits 0..16777215 bytes.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: server_certificate_type in CH/EE versus oid_filters only in CR.
They map different AlertDescription members to different values: bad_certificate to 42 and bad_certificate_hash_value_RESERVED to 114.

The Figure 4 check only orders EndOfEarlyData before client Finished, while the state-machine check triggers after receipt of server Finished and orders EndOfEarlyData before all remaining client handshake messages.
The identical byte range applies to different fields: OIDFilterExtension.filters versus CertificateEntry.extensions.
The opaque vectors are different fields with different minima: DistinguishedName requires 1..65535 bytes, while OIDFilter.certificate_extension_values permits 0..65535 bytes.
Accepting a PSK cipher suite is a prerequisite distinct from verifying that the selected cipher suite exactly matches the suite associated with the selected PSK.
The required ClientHello extensions and conditions differ: supported_versions is generally required, while supported_groups is required for DHE or ECDHE key exchange.
Restricting all PSKs offered in the ClientHello to advertised modes is broader than restricting only PSK resumption to an advertised mode.

The placement-table rule applies to any psk_key_exchange_modes occurrence and permits it only in ClientHello; the normative rule is the narrower directional prohibition on a server sending the extension.
They map different CertificateType members to different values: X509 to 0 and OpenPGP_RESERVED to 1.
They map different CipherSuite members to different wire values: TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 to 0x1303 and TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256 to 0x1304.
The triggers differ: intent to authenticate the server by certificate versus any TLS 1.3 ClientHello that omits pre_shared_key.
The PSK sources and parameter sources differ: externally provisioned PSKs use provisioned 0-RTT parameters, while ticket PSKs inherit them from the connection that issued the ticket.
The vectors carry different element types and declared maxima: SignatureSchemeList is 2..65534 bytes, while NamedGroupList is 2..65535 bytes.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: psk_key_exchange_modes only in CH versus certificate_authorities in CH/CR.
The limits apply to different fields and have different minima: CertificateAuthoritiesExtension.authorities starts at 3 bytes, while CertificateRequest.extensions starts at 2.
The identical byte range applies to different fields: OIDFilterExtension.filters versus EncryptedExtensions.extensions.
The alert outcome matches, but the malformed inputs are separate alternatives: invalid unencrypted change_cipher_spec content versus any protected change_cipher_spec record.

The derivations use different secrets, labels, and transcript endpoints: server_handshake_traffic_secret with 's hs traffic' through ServerHello versus exporter_master_secret with 'exp master' through server Finished.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: signed_certificate_timestamp in CH/CR/CT versus key_share in CH/SH/HRR.
The serialization checks target different structures and fields: TLSPlaintext.fragment versus TLSInnerPlaintext.content.
One states the cross-ticket security outcome after a PSK compromise; the other requires the distinct-key mechanism for multiple tickets. Outcome and mechanism are not the same atomic check.
They map different HandshakeType members to different values: certificate_request to 13 and certificate_status_RESERVED to 22.
They map different ContentType members to different values: invalid to 0 and alert to 21.
The placement checks concern different extensions and message sets: max_fragment_length in CH/EE versus post_handshake_auth only in CH.
They map different AlertDescription members to different values: bad_record_mac to 20 and bad_certificate to 42.
One restricts pre_shared_key to ClientHello or ServerHello; the other separately requires pre_shared_key to be the final extension within ClientHello.
The limits apply to different Certificate fields and widths: certificate_request_context is 0..255 bytes, while certificate_list is 0..16777215 encoded bytes.
The WAIT_EOED inputs and effects differ: early application data keeps the server in WAIT_EOED, while EndOfEarlyData changes the receiving key and enters WAIT_FLIGHT2.
They map different HandshakeType members to different values: server_hello to 2 and certificate to 11.

Both compute Finished.verify_data as a MAC over the same handshake transcript using a key derived from the applicable Base Key; the canonical evidence gives the direct HMAC formula, finished_key, and optional-certificate handling.
